title: Reverse established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that restores adequate opening and blood flow through an already severely calcified native aortic valve while keeping the patient's own valve in place. The intended result is sustained recovery of leaflet mobility and function, rather than merely slower deterioration or replacement of the valve.

As a proposed mechanism, treatment would remove or remodel pathological calcium deposits and associated fibrosis—the stiffened, scar-like tissue that may also limit leaflet movement—while preserving the leaflets' structural integrity. The concept does not specify a proven drug or procedure. Its defining requirement is functional restoration without creating dangerous debris, damaging the leaflets, causing regurgitation, or allowing stenosis to recur.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis: safely and durably restoring a severely calcified native valve would create a fundamentally different treatment option. Successfully treated patients could avoid or defer an operation or transcatheter valve replacement while retaining adequate native-valve function. The benefit depends on achieving sufficient functional recovery; changing a calcium measurement alone would not establish this outcome.

Conditional downstream possibilities include reducing replacement procedures and their associated treatment burden, and expanding options for patients for whom replacement is difficult. Those benefits would depend on treatment safety, durability, accessibility and the range of disease it can treat. Nothing in the supplied evidence establishes that all patients could avoid replacement, that advanced structural damage would always be reversible, or that a future reversal treatment would outperform replacement.

The useful analogy is restoration of a patient's own tissue function. It should not be extended into a claim that dissolving calcium necessarily regenerates a healthy valve. Calcification, fibrosis, leaflet structure and valve mechanics are distinct parts of the proposed problem; success in one would need to translate into safe, durable improvement in the others.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable reversal of established severe calcific obstruction with preservation of a functioning native valve. As a proposed engineering requirement, treatment must alter the material that stiffens the leaflets sufficiently to improve opening, while leaving them strong and flexible enough to open and close repeatedly. The supplied material does not establish a method that achieves this combination.

The proposed barriers include controlling both mineral deposits and associated fibrosis, avoiding leaflet weakening or tearing, and preventing loosened material from embolizing. Improved opening must also preserve closure: a valve that opens more freely but develops clinically important leakage would not satisfy the intended goal. These are coherent design and safety objectives, but their biological details and relative importance were not verified in the retained scientific source.

Durability is a separate unresolved requirement. An initially successful intervention would need to prevent or sufficiently limit renewed calcification, fibrosis and narrowing. Another challenge is establishing the relationship between structural change and clinical benefit: less calcium accumulation, better leaflet movement, improved blood flow and better patient outcomes are related targets, but evidence for one cannot automatically substitute for evidence for the others.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a study titled “Effect of Evogliptin on the Progression of Aortic Valvular Calcification,” attributed to Jae-Kwan Song and colleagues in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, dated 17 September 2024, with DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.06.037. However, the validated review reports that the retained source contained only a cookie-access notice, with no identifiable abstract or scientific results. These bibliographic details are therefore supplied research metadata, rather than details independently confirmed by the review.

The research describes an exploratory randomized trial in which evogliptin did not significantly reduce progression of aortic-valve calcium volume over 96 weeks, while some imaging measures suggested hypotheses for further study. The review could not verify the randomized design, endpoint, 96-week duration, statistical result or exploratory imaging findings because the abstract was absent from the retained copy. These details remain an unverified account of the study; the access failure is not evidence that the account is false. No effect sizes, confidence intervals or sample size are available in the supplied material.

The research characterizes that study as testing slower progression, rather than reversal of established severe stenosis. That characterization also could not be checked against the retained article, but the scientific distinction is essential: even a verified reduction in the rate of calcium accumulation would not demonstrate restoration of a severely obstructed valve. Similarly, exploratory imaging findings would require confirmation and evidence of functional benefit before they could support the proposed innovation.

The supplied research states that valve replacement is established and pharmacological reversal is not. The retained source does not independently substantiate either broad treatment-landscape claim. No verified demonstration of reversal of established severe calcific aortic stenosis is documented in this evidence set, and the empty freshness-search record cannot establish the field's status as of 1 November 2026. This limits the assessment of current progress; it does not establish that reversal is impossible or that no relevant work exists elsewhere.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: controlled studies enrolling patients with established severe calcific aortic stenosis should show clinically meaningful, sustained improvement in valve opening and blood flow through the native valve. Improvement thresholds, measurement methods, patient selection and follow-up duration should be specified in advance. The central test is reversal of existing functional obstruction, rather than slower progression or an isolated change in calcium imaging. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained reversal of severe native aortic valve functional obstruction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and durability requirements: demonstrate preserved leaflet integrity and adequate closure, acceptable embolic and regurgitation risks, and durable benefit without clinically important recurrent stenosis. Structural imaging, functional measurements and clinical outcomes should provide a consistent account of improvement. Follow-up must be long enough to evaluate both early injury and later loss of benefit; the supplied material does not establish an appropriate numerical duration.
completion_criteria.label: Durable valve function with preserved integrity and acceptable risks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical comparison: assess valve replacements, valve-related events, survival and quality of life against appropriate current treatment, with comparators and treatment timing defined for the enrolled population. Avoiding replacement would be convincing only if patients also maintained acceptable function and outcomes. Independent replication and reproducible assessment would strengthen the case, while studies should identify disease stages and patient groups in which treatment fails or remains unsuitable. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not universal reversibility.
completion_criteria.label: Avoided valve replacement with acceptable outcomes versus current treatment

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CAR-02, “Reliably reverse advanced atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree,” shares the ambition to reverse established cardiovascular pathology and may overlap in calcification biology. Its target is arterial disease, whereas CAR-10 targets the structure and opening-and-closing function of a native valve. CAR-12, “Detect actionable coronary plaque risk before a first clinical event,” concerns identifying coronary risk early; detection does not itself reverse valve obstruction.

Roster-based synthesis: CAR-01, “Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart,” and CAR-08, “Durably reverse heart failure with preserved ejection fraction,” overlap with CAR-10 in seeking recovery of native cardiovascular function. Their targets are broader myocardial regeneration and a heart-failure syndrome, respectively. CAR-11, “Reverse pulmonary arterial hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences,” similarly seeks disease reversal but targets the pulmonary circulation and its consequences. Progress in any of these areas would not by itself demonstrate restoration of calcified aortic leaflets.

Roster-based synthesis: CAR-03, “A durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart,” CAR-04, “A dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts,” and CAR-07, “Produce a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart,” address replacement or provision of a whole heart. CAR-10 instead seeks to retain and restore one native valve. These concepts could offer different solutions for different disease burdens and should remain separate innovations.

Roster-based synthesis: CAR-05, “Correct inherited heart disease directly and durably in the beating heart,” shares the goal of durable treatment within the existing heart, but targets inherited disease. CAR-09, “A durable, non-ablative cure for atrial fibrillation,” targets electrical rhythm rather than mechanical valve obstruction. CAR-06, “Make most preventable sudden cardiac deaths predictable and preventable,” and CAR-13, “Broadly prevent cardiac injury from cancer treatment without weakening cancer control,” emphasize prediction or prevention. Their benefits could complement valve treatment, but none is equivalent to reversing established calcific stenosis.

unresolved_issues: The evogliptin article's identity, bibliographic details, randomized design, study population, endpoints, 96-week findings and exploratory imaging results remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The supplied evidence does not independently establish the broader treatment landscape or the field's status as of 1 November 2026.

Clinically meaningful improvement thresholds, follow-up duration, suitable comparators and acceptable embolic, regurgitation and recurrence risks remain undefined.
The extent to which advanced leaflet fibrosis and structural damage can be reversed while preserving durable valve function remains unresolved.

The review's recommendation to replace the trial account entirely with an access-limitation statement was adapted: the reported details were retained as explicitly unverified research claims to preserve useful information without presenting them as confirmed findings.

brief.title: Restoring a hardened heart valve without replacing it
possible: People whose aortic valve—the heart valve that lets blood flow out—has become severely narrowed by calcium could regain adequate blood flow while keeping their own valve. Treatment would restore its ability to open and close, with benefits that last.
why: Patients could avoid or delay valve replacement and its treatment burden. Restoring their own valve would also expand options for people for whom replacement is difficult.

sources.showed: In a randomized trial, evogliptin did not significantly reduce calcium buildup on the valve. Scans measuring active calcification showed improvement, but the main measure of calcium accumulation did not.
sources.quote: This exploratory study did not demonstrate the protective effect of evogliptin on AV calcification.
sources.cited_for: Drug treatment has produced an exploratory imaging signal without demonstrating reduced calcium accumulation.
sources.not_established: The trial did not demonstrate restored opening or blood flow through an already severely narrowed valve.

sources.who: Tania A. Pawade, Mhairi K. Doris, Rong Bing and colleagues
sources.showed: A randomized trial found that neither denosumab nor alendronic acid slowed valve calcium buildup or worsening obstruction compared with placebo, a treatment without the active drug.
sources.quote:
Neither denosumab nor alendronic acid affected progression of aortic valve 
calcification in patients with calcific aortic stenosis.
sources.cited_for: Targeting processes involved in bone turnover did not slow valve disease in this trial.
sources.not_established: These treatments did not demonstrate reversal of established severe narrowing.

sources.who: A. Hedley Brown and Peter G. H. Davies
sources.showed: They used ultrasound, high-frequency vibrations, during surgery to remove calcium from patients' own valves. Two patients had improved valve function after calcium removal and limited cuts to help the valve open.
sources.cited_for: Surgical calcium removal has improved the function of patients' own narrowed valves.
sources.not_established: Brief follow-up in a tiny series does not establish lasting benefit or safety; one valve flap was punctured and repaired.

shown: Brown and Davies reported improved valve function in two patients after surgical calcium removal and limited cuts. This is a direct example of keeping the patient's own valve while relieving obstruction, but follow-up was brief.

Drug trials have not demonstrated reversal. Evogliptin improved a scan measure of active calcification without significantly reducing calcium buildup. Denosumab and alendronic acid did not slow calcium buildup or worsening valve obstruction.
missing: A reliable treatment must restore adequate opening and blood flow through an already severely narrowed valve.
Calcium and scar-like tissue must be altered without weakening the valve, causing leakage or releasing dangerous debris into the bloodstream.
Restored function must last without renewed narrowing and deliver acceptable patient outcomes while avoiding replacement.

milestones.label: Sustained recovery of valve opening and blood flow
milestones.explanation: Controlled studies would have to show lasting, meaningful improvement in patients with established severe calcium-related narrowing. This would demonstrate recovery of function beyond a change on a calcium scan.

milestones.label: Lasting valve function with acceptable risks
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to show intact valve flaps, adequate closure, acceptable risks from loose debris and leakage, and no important recurrent narrowing. This would establish that recovery remains safe and durable.

milestones.label: Fewer replacements with acceptable patient outcomes
milestones.explanation: Comparative trials would have to show fewer replacements with acceptable valve function, survival, valve-related events and quality of life. This would establish whether preserving the valve delivers clinical benefit.

uncertain: Can advanced scarring and structural damage be reversed while leaving valve tissue strong and flexible?
How much improvement, how long a follow-up and what levels of leakage, loose debris and recurrent narrowing would count as success?
Which patients and disease stages could benefit, and which would still require replacement?

page.title: Reversal of severe calcific aortic stenosis
page.definition: Calcium stiffens the aortic valve leaflets and narrows the opening through which the heart pumps blood. Reversal means that the patient’s own valve opens enough for the stenosis to become non-severe and remains functional on follow-up, without replacement or new leakage requiring intervention. Focused ultrasound has increased valve area in patients with severe stenosis, but the mean area at 12 months remained in the severe range among patients with paired measurements.

goal.need: Severe aortic stenosis affected an estimated 3.4% of adults over 75 in seven studies. Among 358 patients unsuitable for surgery, one-year mortality was 50.7% with standard care and 30.7% with transcatheter replacement. Some patients can undergo neither procedure. Balloon dilation can ease symptoms, but its early quality-of-life advantage was lost by one year. Lasting relief with their own valve could help these patients remain active, provided the valve also closes well enough to prevent disabling leakage.

figures.caption: One-year mortality in PARTNER cohort B, reported in 2010
figures.note: Kaplan–Meier estimates in patients unsuitable for surgery. Standard therapy included balloon valvuloplasty. These historical results do not estimate current outcomes for all patients with severe stenosis.

completion.title: A controlled trial confirms reversal of severe native aortic stenosis without replacement.
completion.criterion: In patients with confirmed severe calcific native aortic stenosis, a controlled trial demonstrates treatment-attributable recovery through 12 months: effective valve area >1.0 cm², peak velocity <4.0 m/s and mean gradient <40 mmHg, with integrated imaging excluding residual low-flow severe stenosis. Patients retain their valve without replacement or new regurgitation requiring guideline-directed intervention. The study meets its prospectively specified clinical-benefit and safety endpoints.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis of guideline severity boundaries and registered follow-up, without endorsement of this combined test by the cited bodies.
completion.basis: The Atlas combines guideline severity boundaries with a 12-month interval used in the Valvosoft pivotal study. No external body defines this combined reversal endpoint. In a surgical decalcification series, six of 43 patients assessed at follow-up required replacement for severe leakage. A separate series compared 34 decalcification patients with 68 matched replacement patients and documented improved postoperative valve opening. Neither series establishes the combined endpoint. The single-arm ultrasound study had paired 12-month valve areas for 24 of 60 patients.

milestones.title: Treatment lowers the mean pressure gradient across calcified bioprostheses at 4 L/min (paired p ≤ 0.05).
milestones.criterion: Measure the mean pressure gradient across each explanted calcified bioprosthetic aortic valve before and after treatment at the same flow of 4 L/min. Show a reduction by the Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test at the protocol’s significance level.
milestones.set_by: Villemain et al., experimental protocol for calcified bioprosthetic valves
milestones.threshold_quote: The level of significance was set at an alpha level of ≤0.05.

milestones.title: First-in-human ultrasound treatment increases native valve area and lowers the mean pressure gradient.
milestones.criterion: In patients with severe symptomatic native aortic stenosis, show improved valve opening by comparing echocardiographic valve area and mean pressure gradient with baseline. Assess procedure-related deaths through 30 days. The published pooled report gives no minimum improvement required in either echocardiographic measure.
milestones.set_by: Messas et al., pooled first-in-human Valvosoft studies NCT03779620 and NCT04665596
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary endpoints were procedure-related deaths within 30 days and improved valve function.

milestones.title: A native-valve treatment keeps the upper 95% confidence bound for 30-day major adverse events below 25%.
milestones.criterion: For the frail population with severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis enrolled under the Valvosoft pivotal protocol, the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the 30-day composite event rate must be below 25%. The composite includes all-cause death, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, stroke, major or life-threatening bleeding, and hospitalization for heart failure. Report the separate primary performance endpoint as the proportion whose New York Heart Association functional class improves at 30 days.
milestones.set_by: Cardiawave, NCT05235568; the prespecified confidence-bound test is described by Vincent et al. This safety target was set for a frail population unsuitable for valve replacement.
milestones.threshold_quote: with the upper CI bound below the 25% event rate considered acceptable for this frail population

milestones.title: A native aortic valve remains non-severely stenotic at 12 months without replacement.
milestones.criterion: Document relief of initially severe calcific stenosis in the same patient through 12 months. At 12 months the native valve has an effective area >1.0 cm², peak velocity <4.0 m/s and mean gradient <40 mmHg. Integrated imaging excludes residual low-flow severe stenosis. The patient has retained the valve without new regurgitation requiring intervention.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. No external body defines this combined patient-level milestone. ESC/EACTS supplies the diagnostic boundaries and NCT05235568 supplies the follow-up interval.

milestones.title: Calcific deposits can be removed from an excised human aortic valve without damaging adjacent tissue.
milestones.criterion: Apply ultrasonic debridement to a calcified human aortic valve excised at surgery. Demonstrate removal of mineral deposits with the adjacent normal leaflet tissue intact.
milestones.set_by: A. Hedley Brown and Peter G. H. Davies, preliminary excised-valve experiment
milestones.threshold_quote: removing the calcification without adjacent damage or loss of suture-holding tissue

milestones.title: Ultrasound reaches the porcine aortic valve through the chest, with safety assessed through one month.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate transthoracic delivery of focused ultrasound to the aortic valve in living swine. Compare treated and sham animals for adverse effects during treatment and at one month, including arrhythmia, valve dysfunction, thrombosis and injury to the valve or surrounding tissue. The protocol specifies follow-up but gives no numerical acceptable event rate.
milestones.set_by: Messas et al., porcine feasibility and safety protocol
milestones.threshold_quote: Secondary objectives: occurrence, severity and evolution of side effects during therapy and at 1 month follow-up.

not_found: No published consensus or regulatory test combining reversal of severe native-valve obstruction, safety and durability was found.
No consensus duration establishing durability of native-valve reversal was found; 12 months is a registered assessment interval.
The 2023 Lancet full text was inaccessible; its indexed PubMed abstract was available.
ClinicalTrials.gov pages did not render their complete records; indexed registry text supplied the endpoint descriptions.

results.finding: Ultrasonic debridement removed mineral deposits from 3 excised human aortic valves with normal tissue intact.
results.detail: Interstitial cartilaginous deposits were harder to remove. The authors cautioned that the sharp probe tip could tear tissue.

results.finding: Two patients had native aortic valve debridement with commissurotomy. One had a follow-up pressure gradient of 24 mmHg.
results.detail: The reported gradient came from ventricular and aortic pressure traces. Both patients also underwent commissurotomy.

results.finding: Two patients retained their native aortic valves after surgical debridement, with follow-up extending to 3 months.
Among 15 treated calcified bioprostheses, leaflet surfaces were intact and micro-CT estimated a 2.02% decrease in calcification volume.
results.detail: Micro-CT showed internal fragmentation without a statistically significant change in calcium volume. The text does not specify the number of valves in the micro-CT analysis.
results.quote: The histological analyses showed a fragmentation of calcifications with the preservation of the leaflet superficial structures.

results.finding: In 8 explanted calcified aortic bioprostheses at 4 L/min, ultrasound lowered the mean pressure gradient (reported p < 0.001).
results.detail: The reported p < 0.001 cannot arise from an exact signed-rank test on 8 valve-level pairs. The minimum exact two-sided p is 0.0078, which is below the criterion’s 0.05 threshold. The verdict follows the paper’s reported analysis.
results.quote: After the procedure, the mean transvalvular gradient was 9.6 ± 1.7 mm Hg (maximum 19 mm Hg; minimum 4 mm Hg), corresponding to a decrease of 55 ± 10% (p < 0.001).

results.finding: In a cohort of 40 adults with severe symptomatic native aortic stenosis, mean valve area increased 10% at 6 months after transthoracic ultrasound.
results.detail: The abstract gives the enrollment count but does not specify how many patients contributed paired echocardiographic measurements.
results.quote: Improved valve function was confirmed up to 6 months, reflected by a 10% increase in mean aortic valve area from 0·58 cm 2  (SD 0·19) at baseline to 0·64 cm 2  (0·21) at follow-up (p=0·0088), and a 7% decrease in mean pressure gradient from 41·9 mm Hg (20·1) to 38·8 mm Hg (17·8; p=0·024).

results.finding: In 29 pivotal-study patients with paired echocardiograms, mean aortic gradient fell to 34.3 mmHg at 12 months.
results.detail: At the last available follow-up, the mean gradient fell from 36.3 to 33.4 mmHg (n=52, p=0.050), with a median follow-up of 361 days.
results.quote: mean gradient improved from 37.0±12.6 to 34.3±11.6 mm Hg

edit m2: title = "First-in-human ultrasound treatment increases native valve area and lowers the mean pressure gradient."; criterion = "In patients with severe symptomatic native aortic stenosis, show improved valve opening by comparing echocardiographic valve area and mean pressure gradient with baseline. Assess procedure-related deaths through 30 days. The published pooled report gives no minimum improvement required in either echocardiographic measure."; set_by = "Messas et al., pooled first-in-human Valvosoft studies NCT03779620 and NCT04665596"; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "The primary endpoints were procedure-related deaths within 30 days and improved valve function."; threshold_ref = 9; refs = [9]. Reason: The functional endpoint becomes interpretable when the direction of change in valve area and pressure gradient is stated separately from the observed effect sizes.

edit m3: criterion = "For the frail population with severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis enrolled under the Valvosoft pivotal protocol, the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the 30-day composite event rate must be below 25%. The composite includes all-cause death, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, stroke, major or life-threatening bleeding, and hospitalization for heart failure. Report the separate primary performance endpoint as the proportion whose New York Heart Association functional class improves at 30 days."; threshold_quote = "with the upper CI bound below the 25% event rate considered acceptable for this frail population"; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [4, 10]. Reason: The criterion should specify the pivotal safety rule and its population without using the observed event rate or symptom response as thresholds.

edit m4: criterion = "Document relief of initially severe calcific stenosis in the same patient through 12 months. At 12 months the native valve has an effective area >1.0 cm\u00b2, peak velocity <4.0 m/s and mean gradient <40 mmHg. Integrated imaging excludes residual low-flow severe stenosis. The patient has retained the valve without new regurgitation requiring intervention."; set_by = "Technology Atlas. No external body defines this combined patient-level milestone. ESC/EACTS supplies the diagnostic boundaries and NCT05235568 supplies the follow-up interval."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; refs = [2, 4, 10, 12, 13]. Reason: The 12-month criterion needs measurements from the same patient because cohort means cannot establish that an individual retained a functioning valve.
